chances.note: If the US goes 14 days without striking Iran starting by Dec 31 (Polymarket puts that near 0.71), the low-level exchange has cooled and Trump's Nov 8 line holds: restarting the war is 'highly unlikely' if talks produce a strong agreement. Ceasefires in April and June both broke down within weeks, so a pause still leaves about one chance in five of an extensive round by May.

If US strikes continue through December with no 14-day pause, the flare-up Rabobank describes ('ships are still being attacked and President Trump is yet again considering plans for another round of extensive strikes') has not cooled, and Israel is pressing for action against Iran's rebuilt missile stock. An extensive round by May is then about even.

passages: Global benchmark Brent has retreated by more than a fifth so far this month, as supplies from the Middle East recovered and Trump held off on renewed large-scale strikes against the Islamic Republic. Still, there’s been a flare-up in low-level fighting across the region in recent days, including a spate of attacks on vessels transiting the critical Strait of Hormuz.

“We are not yet at the point where the narrative of improving supply is enough to overshadow the military flare-ups in the region,” said Florence Schmit, a senior energy strategist at Rabobank. “Flows through Hormuz have improved, yet ships are still being attacked and President Trump is yet again considering plans for another round of extensive strikes on Iran.”

to.title: No extensive strikes and no nuclear deal: the standoff continues
to.text: Through May 18, 2027 the US launches no new round of extensive strikes on Iran and the two sign no nuclear deal: limited exchanges and talks continue, and Gulf supply keeps recovering at its current pace.
to.resolution_source: US government; consensus of major news reporting

to.title: The US and Iran sign a nuclear deal with no extensive strikes first
to.text: By May 18, 2027 the United States and Iran agree a nuclear deal that limits Iran's programme in exchange for sanctions relief, without a new round of extensive US strikes before it.
to.resolution_source: US and Iranian government statements; consensus of major news reporting

chances.note: Kalshi asks a deal before July 1, 2027. May 18 is 180 of the 224 days to that deadline, and Kalshi's own ladder puts 0.095 of its 0.205 before March 1, so about three quarters of deals by July land by May 18; of those, I take 0.85 to come without an extensive round of strikes first. 0.75 x 0.85 is about 0.62.

shock.note: A deal brings sanctions relief for Iranian barrels and ends the threat to Hormuz. Crude already fell 19% from Oct 30 to Nov 18 as Gulf supply recovered (window) and Saxo notes 'renewing concerns about an emerging supply glut'; a signed deal takes Brent from about $92 toward the high $70s, 15% below the standoff.

Energy costs are driving inflation here and abroad (euro-area 4.0%, 'with energy costs driving both'), and that inflation is why the Fed is raising rates. Cheaper oil eases both; I put the S&P 2% above the standoff.
Lower oil takes some inflation premium out of long yields: about a third of the 0.22-point rise seen when the war began (window), in reverse.

Exxon fell 13.8% while crude fell 19% from Oct 30 to Nov 18 (window), about 0.7 of oil's move. For a further 15% in oil I use 8%, a little over half, since part of the war premium has already left the shares.

Brent 'has retreated by more than a fifth so far this month, as supplies from the Middle East recovered and Trump held off on renewed large-scale strikes'. An extensive round reverses that: Iran has warned neighbours of retaliation and ships in Hormuz are already under attack. The first month of the war lifted crude 61% (window); with Gulf flows now partly rerouted and the market practised, I use 22%, roughly back to late October's level.
passages: Global benchmark Brent has retreated by more than a fifth so far this month, as supplies from the Middle East recovered and Trump held off on renewed large-scale strikes against the Islamic Republic.

shock.note: The S&P lost 3.2% over the first month of the war while crude rose 61% (window). A smaller oil move this time, but into a Fed that is already raising rates against energy-led inflation; I keep 3%.

Long yields rose 0.22 points in the war's first month as oil fed inflation expectations (window); about half of that for an oil move about a third the size, since rate-rise fears are now more sensitive.

Exxon gained 7.6% in the war's first month, far less than its measured link to crude implied, because the market treated the spike as temporary (window); on the way down this month it lost 13.8% for 19% in crude. For crude 22% higher I use 8%.

markets.question: Will the US agree to a new Iranian nuclear deal this year?
markets.rules:
If the United States has agreed to, signed, or accepted a new Iran-US nuclear deal before Jul 1, 2027, then the market resolves to Yes.

An agreement also made with other countries (i.e. multilaterally) is still encompassed if the United States participates. "A new Iran-US nuclear deal" means a formal written agreement signed by authorized representatives of both the United States and Iran that (1) imposes verifiable restrictions on Iran's nuclear program, including limits on uranium enrichment, centrifuge numbers, or nuclear facility operations, AND (2) provides for the lifting, suspension, or modification of at least one US economic sanction on Iran in exchange for Iran's nuclear commitments.

Clarification (04/19/26): The Agreement Long rulebook variable defines the nature of the qualifying instrument: it must be a formal written agreement signed by authorized representatives of both governments. It does not impose a precondition that the signing itself must occur before resolution. Because the Payout Criterion is satisfied if the United States has "agreed to, signed, or accepted" such an instrument, both governments publicly and officially agreeing to the terms of what will be a qualifying written agreement is sufficient to resolve the market to Yes, even if the formal signing has not yet taken place.

Clarification (06/02/26): A qualifying instrument must impose "verifiable restrictions on Iran's nuclear program." A restriction is "verifiable" only where it establishes a concrete, objectively ascertainable standard (a defined limit, prohibition, quantity, or monitoring provision) against which compliance could in principle be confirmed; a general expression of intent that fixes no such standard is not considered “verifiable” for the purposes of this event. Accordingly, a bare pledge not to develop or pursue nuclear weapons, unaccompanied by any concrete limit on Iran's nuclear materials, activities, or facilities, does not on its own satisfy criterion (1). Conversely, a commitment to completely 'stop' or ‘suspend’ a specific nuclear activity (such as uranium enrichment) establishes a concrete prohibition (an implicit limit of zero) and qualifies as a restriction, whereas a vague promise to 'reduce' activities without a defined metric or monitoring mechanism does not. The enumerated examples (limits on uranium enrichment, centrifuge numbers, or nuclear facility operations) are illustrative and not exhaustive: a formal, verifiable commitment to remove, transfer, or cap Iran's stock of enriched uranium, confirmable by the receiving state or an oversight body, is a restriction on Iran's nuclear program and satisfies criterion (1). In every case, criterion (2) must independently be met.

Clarification (06/17/26): To clarify, the U.S.–Iran memorandum of understanding reportedly now in effect does not satisfy criterion (1) of the definition of a "new Iran-US nuclear deal," and this market will therefore not resolve to Yes on the basis of that instrument at this time. The memorandum provides for the existing state of Iran's nuclear program to be maintained pending a subsequent agreement, and defers the disposition of Iran's stockpile of enriched uranium to a mechanism to be mutually agreed in that subsequent agreement. That it states a minimum methodology for that future mechanism — down-blending on site under IAEA supervision — constrains the form of a mechanism yet to be agreed, but specifies no quantity, enrichment level, or completion deadline for the down-blending. An instrument that provides for maintaining Iran's nuclear program at an unspecified status quo, or that defers its substantive nuclear commitments to a subsequent agreement, does not by itself establish the concrete, objectively ascertainable standard that a "verifiable" restriction requires.
